extracted.intended_audience: authors, editors, and copyeditors preparing scholarly or formal publications
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and guidance for correct punctuation (periods, commas, colons, semicolons, dashes, hyphens, parentheses, brackets, ellipses, quotation marks, apostrophes, etc.) in scholarly/formal writing, with examples and exceptions. Intended to govern typesetting, editorial decisions, and manuscript preparation.

rubrics_metrics.name: No period after Roman numerals
rubrics_metrics.description: Use no period after Roman numerals, even if having the value of ordinals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Vol. IV; Louis XVI was on the throne.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit period after running-heads and certain heads
rubrics_metrics.description: Omit the period after running-heads; after centered headlines; after side-heads set in separate lines; after cut-in heads; after box-heads in tables; and after superscriptions and legends which do not form a complete sentence; after date lines at top of communications, and after signatures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See cross-reference to section 50 for related rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Period placement with quotation marks and parentheses
rubrics_metrics.description: The period is placed inside the quotation marks; and inside the parentheses when the matter inclosed is an independent sentence and forms no part of the preceding sentence; otherwise outside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule stated as without exception: Tennyson’s “In Memoriam.” Put the period inside the quotation marks. When parentheses form part of preceding sentence, put the period outside.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the exclamation point
rubrics_metrics.description: The exclamation point is used to mark an outcry, or an emphatic or ironical utterance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: “Long live the king!” “Heaven forbid!” The exclamation point is placed inside quotation marks or parentheses when part of the quotation or parenthetical matter; otherwise outside.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the interrogation point (question mark)
rubrics_metrics.description: The interrogation point is used to mark a query, or to express a doubt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: “Who is this?” Indirect questions should not be followed by an interrogation point: He asked whether he was ill. Place the interrogation point inside quotation marks or parentheses only when it is a part of the quotation or parenthetical matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colon: general function and uses
rubrics_metrics.description: The colon marks a discontinuity of grammatical construction greater than that indicated by the semicolon and less than that indicated by the period; commonly used (1) to emphasize a close connection between two clauses each of which forms a complete sentence; (2) to separate a complete clause from one giving illustration or amplification; (3) to introduce a formal statement, an extract, a speech in dialogue, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before the quotation of a clause in the middle of a sentence use a comma. Examples illustrate each use. Where an implied 'namely' or similar phrase would be used, follow by colon if what follows are grammatically complete clauses; otherwise use a comma.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colon after salutatory phrase and for scripture/time/publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Put a colon after the salutatory phrase at the beginning of a letter and after the introductory remark of a speaker addressing chairman or audience; put a centered colon between chapter and verse in Scripture passages and between hours and minutes in time indications; put a colon between place of publication and publisher’s name in bibliographical references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: My DEAR Mr. Brown: ; Mr. Chairman, Ladies, and Gentlemen: ; Matt. 2:5-13; 4:30 P.M.; Clement of Alexandria (London: Macmillan), II, 97.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colon placement relative to quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: The colon should be placed outside the quotation marks, unless it is a part of the quotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: He writes under the head of 'Notes and Comments': 'Many a man...'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semicolon: general usage
rubrics_metrics.description: A semicolon is used to mark the division of a sentence somewhat more independent than that marked by a comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show linking fairly independent clauses and joining contrasted or parallel clauses. 'For' in such cases should commonly be preceded by a semicolon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semicolon in complex enumerations
rubrics_metrics.description: In enumerations use a semicolon between different links if these consist of more than a few words closely connected, especially if individual clauses contain internal punctuation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example given with membership list where some items contain parenthetical material; also listing defendant's pleas numbered with semicolons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semicolon in scripture references and placement
rubrics_metrics.description: In Scripture references a semicolon is used to separate passages containing chapters; the semicolon should be placed outside quotation marks or parentheses, unless part of the quoted or parenthetical matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma: general definition
rubrics_metrics.description: The comma is 'used to indicate the smallest interruptions in continuity of thought or grammatical construction, the marking of which contributes to clearness.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many illustrative examples demonstrate subtle distinctions of meaning produced by comma placement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma to separate proper nouns belonging to different individuals/places
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a comma to separate proper nouns belonging to different individuals or places.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'To John, Smith was always kind'; 'To America, Europe awards the prize of mechanical skill.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Serial comma before conjunctions in lists (Oxford-comma rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Put a comma before 'and,' 'or,' and 'nor' connecting the last two links in a sequence of three or more; or all the links in a series of greater length, or where each individual link consists of several words; always put a comma before 'etc.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Tom, Dick, and Harry; either copper, silver, or gold; always use comma before etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit comma when conjunction connects brief close-knit phrase
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use a comma where 'and,' etc., serves to connect all the links in a brief and close-knit phrase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'a man good and noble and true'; 'whether it was Shelley or Keats or Moore.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma before/after clauses introduced by conjunctions when subject changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinarily put a comma before and after clauses introduced by conjunctions such as 'and,' 'but,' 'if,' 'while,' 'as,' 'whereas,' 'since,' 'because,' 'when,' 'after,' 'although,' etc., especially if a change of subject takes place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long example showing multiple clauses separated by commas to preserve clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use comma when preceding clause is not logically complete
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use a comma before clauses introduced by such conjunctions if the preceding clause is not logically complete without them; nor before 'if,' 'but,' and 'though' in brief and close-welded phrases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'This is good because true'; 'I shall agree to this only if you accept my conditions'; 'honest though poor.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Commas with introductory adverbs/particles (now, then, however, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Words or phrases like 'now,' 'then,' 'however,' 'indeed,' 'therefore,' 'moreover,' 'nevertheless,' 'for example,' 'that is,' etc., should be followed by a comma when standing at the beginning of a sentence or clause to introduce an inference or explanation, and should be placed between commas when wedged into the middle of a sentence to mark off a distinct break.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Indeed, this was exactly the point...'; 'He thought, however, that he would like to try.' Exceptions follow when connection is close (e.g., 'Therefore I say unto you').

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions for comma with adverbs (close connections)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use a comma with such words when the connection is logically close and structurally smooth enough not to call for any pause in reading; with 'therefore,' 'nevertheless,' etc., when directly following the verb; with 'indeed' when directly preceding or following adjective/adverb it qualifies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Therefore I say unto you'; 'He was therefore unable to be present'; 'He is recovering very slowly indeed.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit comma before 'rather' in certain expressions
rubrics_metrics.description: A comma is preferably omitted before 'rather' in expressions like 'measured in this way rather than by...'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'The time-value is to be measured in this way rather than by the time-equivalent of the strata.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma between coordinate adjectives
rubrics_metrics.description: If among several adjectives preceding a noun the last bears a more direct relation to the noun than the others, it should not be preceded by a comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the admirable political institutions of the country' (no comma before 'political'); 'a handsome, wealthy young man' (comma between first two adjectives).

rubrics_metrics.name: Participial clauses usually set off by commas
rubrics_metrics.description: Participial clauses, especially those that contain an explanation of the main clause, should usually be set off by commas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Being asleep, he did not hear him'; 'Exhausted by a hard day's work, he slept like a stone.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma before 'not' introducing an antithetical clause
rubrics_metrics.description: Put a comma before 'not' when it introduces an antithetical clause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Men addict themselves to inferior pleasures, not because they deliberately prefer them...'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use commas for parenthetical/adverbial/appositional clauses; prefer dashes for strongly independent interpolations
rubrics_metrics.description: For parenthetical, adverbial, or appositional clauses or phrases use commas to indicate structurally disconnected but logically integral interpolations; use dashes to indicate both structurally and logically disconnected insertions; never use the two together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples contrasting commas vs. dashes; cross-reference to other sections (150, 167).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma to indicate omission (elliptical constructions)
rubrics_metrics.description: A comma is employed to indicate the omission, for brevity or convenience, of a word or words the repetition of which is not essential to the meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'In Illinois there are seventeen such institutions; in Ohio, twenty-two; in Indiana, thirteen.' Often such constructions may be smooth enough not to call for commas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma with brief direct quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: A direct quotation, maxim, or similar expression, when brief, should be separated from the preceding part of the sentence by a comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'God said, Let there be light.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma with 'of' in residence or position
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a comma before 'of' in connection with residence or position (e.g., Mr. and Mrs. McIntyre, of Detroit, Mich.; President Hadley, of Yale University).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions where place-name practically is part of person's name: Clement of Alexandria, Philip of Anjou.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commas and page/date formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use a comma between consecutive pages in literary references; use en dash; separate month and year by a comma; put commas after digits indicating thousands except when used as a date or in a page reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: pp. 4, 7-8, 10; November, 1905; 1,270; note that some journals print four-figure years without comma.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit comma in signatures and at article beginnings
rubrics_metrics.description: Omit the comma in signatures and at the beginning of articles after author’s name followed by address, title, or position in a separate line, or after address followed by a date line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given showing names, titles, addresses on separate lines without comma.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma placement relative to quotation marks and parentheses
rubrics_metrics.description: The comma is always placed inside the quotation marks, but following the parentheses, if the context requires it at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference to other rules and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apostrophe for contractions and omission
rubrics_metrics.description: An apostrophe is used to mark the omission of a letter or letters in the contraction of a word, or of figures in a number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ne'er, don't, 'twas; the class of '96. See section 123 for further guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possessive case formation with apostrophe
rubrics_metrics.description: The possessive case of nouns, common and proper, is formed by the addition of an apostrophe, or apostrophe and s, with rules for singular/plural and sibilant endings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a man's word, horses' tails; Scott's Ivanhoe, Jones's farms, Themistocles' era; for appearance' sake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plural of numerals and rare coinages with apostrophe
rubrics_metrics.description: The plural of numerals, and of rare or artificial noun-coinages, is formed by the aid of an apostrophe and s; proper nouns of more than one syllable ending in a sibilant add apostrophe alone; monosyllabic proper names ending in s add 's.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: in the 1900's; the three R's; the Y.M.C.A.'s; all the Tommy Atkins' of England (but the Rosses...).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotation marks: placement cross-referenced
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules for quotation marks are provided in the section on 'Quotations' (see 74-91).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See indicated section for comprehensive rules on single vs double, placement of punctuation, block quotes, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dash: general usage
rubrics_metrics.description: A dash denotes a sudden break, stop, or transition in a sentence, an abrupt change in construction, a long or significant pause, or an unexpected/epigrammatic turn of sentiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Do we—can we—send out educated boys and girls...?' Use dashes for strong parenthetical clauses that are logically and structurally independent. Repeated examples and cross-references to related rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dash to introduce emphasis or repeated element
rubrics_metrics.description: A clause added to lend emphasis to, or to explain or expand, a word or phrase occurring in the main clause, which word or phrase is then repeated, should be introduced by a dash.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'To him they are more important as the sources for history—the history of events and ideas.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Dash when 'namely' is implied and sentence-final summarizing clause
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a 'namely' is implied before a parenthetical or complementary clause, a dash should preferably be used; in sentences broken into clauses, the final summarizing clause should be preceded by a dash.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'These discoveries—gunpowder, printing-press, compass, and telescope—were...'; multi-clause example with dash before final clause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dash for separate-line lead-ins and side-heads
rubrics_metrics.description: A word or phrase set in a separate line and succeeded by paragraphs at the beginning of each of which it is implied should be followed by a dash; use a dash in connection with side-heads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show paragraph enumerations and side-heads followed by dashes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use en dash versus em dash for ranges and breaks
rubrics_metrics.description: Use en dash for simple ranges (May–July, pp. 3–7) and em dash for sentence breaks; use dash as replacement for 'to' connecting two words or numbers; rules for omitting hundreds in consecutive numbers explained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: May–July, 1906 (en dash); May 1, 1905—November 1, 1906 (em dash); pp. 3–7 (en dash). Guidance on omitting hundreds in ranges and exceptions for B.C. dates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using dash with other punctuation except period
rubrics_metrics.description: A dash should not ordinarily be used in connection with any other point, except a period; avoid combining dashes and commas in certain constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorrect examples shown to illustrate misuse (e.g., 'DEAR SIR:—I have the honor...' discouraged).

rubrics_metrics.name: Parentheses for enumerative divisions and sparing use
rubrics_metrics.description: Place between parentheses figures or letters used to mark divisions in enumerations run into the text; if such divisions are paragraphed, a single parenthesis is ordinarily used with lowercase letters or a period with figures/capital letters. Parentheses should not ordinarily be used for parenthetical clauses unless confusion would result or the clause is wholly irrelevant to main argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: '(1) advanced age, (2) failing health...' and guidance on layout schemes (A., 1., a), (a)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Brackets: uses
rubrics_metrics.description: Brackets are used (1) to inclose an explanation or note, (2) to indicate an interpolation in a quotation, (3) to rectify a mistake, (4) to supply an omission, and (5) for parentheses within parentheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided for each numbered use; phrases like '[Continued from p. 320]' should be bracketed, centered, italicized, and set in reduced type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ellipses: indicate omission and formatting rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Ellipses indicate the omission from a quotation of one or more words not essential to the idea, and to indicate illegible words, mutilations, and other lacunae. For an ellipsis at the beginning, middle, or end of a sentence four periods, separated by a space (en quad), should ordinarily be used (except in French three only). If the preceding line ends in a point, this should not be included in the four.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where whole paragraphs or lines are omitted, insert a full line of periods separated by em- or 2-em quads, not extending beyond the longest type-line. Ellipsis should be treated as part of the citation and enclosed in quotation marks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphen at line breaks and between many compound words
rubrics_metrics.description: A hyphen is placed at the end of a line terminating with a syllable of a word carried to the next line, and between many compound words according to provided rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See extensive rules below about hyphenation of compound adjectives before nouns, use of en dash when component contains more than one word, and many specific compound classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate compound adjectives before a noun
rubrics_metrics.description: Hyphenate two or more words (except proper names forming a unity) combined into one adjective preceding a noun, or when the noun is understood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: well-known author, first-class investment, better-trained teachers, high-school course, four-year-old boy, up-to-date machinery; but: New Testament times, Old English spelling (no hyphen when following noun).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use en dash between compound elements when a component contains more than one word
rubrics_metrics.description: Where one of the components contains more than one word, use an en dash in place of a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: New York–Chicago freight traffic; Norwegian–German–Jewish immigrant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not hyphenate adverb + adjective when adverb ends in -ly or when following noun
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not connect by a hyphen adjectives or participles with adverbs ending in '-ly'; nor such combinations when following the noun, or qualifying a predicate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: highly developed species; a man well known in the neighborhood; Her gown was up to date (no hyphen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate noun compounds in objective relation, with exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Hyphenate, as a rule, nouns formed by combination of two nouns standing in objective relation (one component derived from transitive verb); exceptions include common brief compounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: mind-reader, story-teller, office-holder; exceptions: lawgiver, taxpayer, proofreader, bookkeeper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphen with present participle + noun formations
rubrics_metrics.description: A present participle united with a noun to form a new noun with a distinct meaning should have a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: boarding-house, dining-hall, sleeping-room, stepping-stone, working-man.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules for compounds with book/house/mill/room/work
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'book,' 'house,' 'mill,' 'room,' 'shop,' and 'work' generally printed as one word when the prefixed noun has one syllable, hyphenated when it contains two, and printed as two separate words when it contains three or more, with stated exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: handbook, pocket-book, bookstore; boathouse, power-house; cornmill, water-mill; bedroom, classroom, lecture-room; handwork, woodwork; exceptions noted for rare formations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compounds of 'maker', 'dealer', and occupation words usually hyphenated
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'maker', 'dealer', and words denoting occupation should ordinarily be hyphenated; nouns denoting different occupations of same individual should be hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: harness-maker, book-dealer, job-printer; soldier-statesman, poet-artist Rossetti. Short everyday exceptions: bookmaker, dressmaker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenation rules for kinship and degree terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'fellow' are always hyphenated; compounds of 'father', 'mother', 'brother', 'sister', 'daughter', 'parent', 'foster' should be hyphenated when forming the first element; compounds of 'great' indicating degree use hyphen; compounds of 'life' and 'world' require hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: fellow-man; mother-tongue; great-grandfather; life-history; world-power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules for 'self-' and number-fold combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'self' when first element are hyphenated; combinations with 'fold' are one word if the number has one syllable, two words if it contains more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: self-evident; twofold, tenfold; fifteen fold, a hundred fold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjectives formed with '-like' and hyphenation
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjectives formed by suffixing 'like' to a noun usually printed as one word if noun is one syllable (except when ending in l); if noun contains more or is proper, hyphenate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: childlike, homelike, godlike; wheel-like, American-like (but Christlike).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenation of titles with 'Vice', 'ex', 'elect', 'general', 'lieutenant'
rubrics_metrics.description: Words 'Vice', 'ex', 'elect', 'general', and 'lieutenant' that are parts of titles should be connected with the chief noun by a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Vice-Consul Taylor, ex-President Cleveland, the governor-elect, the postmaster-general, a lieutenant-colonel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenation with by- compounds and particle prefixes
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'by-' should be hyphenated; prefixes 'co-','pre-','re-' take a hyphen when followed by the same vowel as they end in or by w or y, but as a rule not when followed by a different vowel or a consonant; exceptions for proper names, unusual formations, or cases where omission changes meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: by-product, co-operation, pre-empted, re-enter; but: coequal, prearranged, recast. Exceptions: pre-Raphaelite, re-formation vs reformation, re-cover vs recover.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenation for negatives, quasi-, over-/under- and Latin prepositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Negative particles 'un-','in-','a-' usually do not require hyphen; 'non-' ordinarily takes a hyphen except in common words; 'quasi-' requires hyphen; 'over' and 'under' usually do not require hyphen except unusual cases; Latin prepositions ante/anti/inter/intra/post/sub/super do not ordinarily require hyphen but have exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: unmanly, indeterminate, non-essential (hyphen), quasi-corporation, overbold (no hyphen), antebellum (exception ante-bellum).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate fractional spelled-out numbers and indicate omitted common elements by hyphen
rubrics_metrics.description: In fractional numbers spelled out, connect numerator and denominator with a hyphen unless either already contains a hyphen; when two or more compound words occur together and share a component, indicate the omitted common element by a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: two-thirds, four and five-sevenths; in English- and German-speaking countries; one-, five-, and ten-cent pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphen is used to indicate prefixes/suffixes or syllabication
rubrics_metrics.description: A hyphen indicates a prefix or suffix, as a particle or syllable, not complete in itself; also used to indicate syllables of a word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the prefix a-; suffixes -chen and -lein; di-a-gram, pho-tog-ra-phy.
